text: Scoring your environment against a maturity model isn't a survey you fill out from memory. It's an evidence-gathering exercise that forces you to answer one question honestly for each pillar: can you prove this is true in production today, for essentially the whole relevant population — not the pilot group, not the showcase app?

A workable process has four steps. Isolate one pillar at a time, so you don't blur five pillars into one vague impression. Start from the Optimal stage definition and work backward, dropping a stage until you hit one you can actually prove. Score to the evidence you have, not the plan — a signed charter for next quarter is not proof of today's maturity. And score coverage, not capability: a tool enforcing compliance on 40% of endpoints earns a 40% score, not credit for being 'Advanced-capable.'

Here's Identity worked through. Optimal would mean continuous, risk-based access evaluated on every single request, everywhere — but service accounts and a handful of legacy apps still bypass it entirely, so that's a no. Advanced would mean phishing-resistant MFA and automated risk scoring — and that's mostly true, enforced for every admin and roughly seventy percent of standard users. The honest score is Advanced, with a documented gap in legacy apps and non-human identity, not rounded up to a clean label.

Four mistakes show up constantly in self-scoring, and all of them make an organization look more mature than it is. Scoring the tool instead of the behavior — owning a PAM platform doesn't mean the rollout finished. Scoring the showcase system — one app with full zero-trust controls doesn't represent the forty legacy ones behind it. Averaging instead of reporting the floor. And scoring intent as if it were already fact.

Devices makes the floor point concrete. Managed laptops get automated inventory, patching, and compliance checks feeding every access decision — genuinely Advanced. But unmanaged BYOD devices have no compliance signal at all, and they're still allowed limited access anyway. The honest pillar score is whichever path actually governs your real risk, and that's the weaker one, because that's the door that's actually open.

Score the evidence, record the specific gap, and resist rounding up — that discipline is what makes a maturity score something another engineer, or an executive, can actually act on. Next lesson turns that same discipline toward metrics: the numbers that prove zero trust is reducing real risk, not just that you implemented something.
